Regarding the commentary on the *Lanpen jing* by our ancestor, Chan Master Guifeng: its profundity is such that among the authors of antiquity, none can rival it; when lectured upon, it is unsurpassed.

The transmission and circulation [of this text] has long been established; Venerable Shibi first composed a record for it, and Master Gushan followed his explanation to extensively expound upon the corroborating meanings. Master Zhiyuan Jin also subsequently produced such a description.
Since the emergence of Master Gushan’s new commentary, the old record of Shibi has no longer circulated in the world, as people have come to prefer literary elegance. I have humbly...
I have once combined various commentaries and applied my utmost thought and refinement, yet the "Harmony of Jade" and the "Pearl of Sui" each boast of their own achievements.

This is truly because, regarding whether the teachings one follows are sound or flawed, and whether the literary meanings are rejected or accepted, it is difficult to achieve that which is ultimately perfect.
Did not the former sages say: "What we hope for is that those of later generations will diagnose the present, just as the present diagnoses the past"? Therefore...
I, lacking self-restraint, have ventured to apply my clumsy abilities to rectify this work, hoping that public judgment may find some ground for it.
Thus, I have collated the ancient with the modern and inscribed its title; may those who know me not reproach me for this derisive imitation of others’ follies?
*Annotative Record of the "Commentary on the Ullambana Sūtra": Harmonizing the Ancient and Illuminating the Present*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Great Master Puguang (Wugji), Puguang.

The explanation of the commentary is divided into two parts: first, the title; second, the main body of the commentary. Regarding the title, there are five characters consisting of both retained and omitted elements.

Regarding the threefold discernment of subject and object through mutual exclusion: first, within the commentary itself, the *Sūtra* (the text) is the subject that explains, while all other elements are the objects explained.
Second, within the objects explained, the *Sūtra* is the subject that expresses, while all else belongs to the expressed content.

Third, within the expressed content, the "bowl" (*pen*) is the subject that rescues, while "Ullambana" is the object to be rescued. If one follows the title of the original sūtra by adding "Spoken by the Buddha," then "speaking" (*shuo*) applies universally.

The relationship between the subject and the object can be understood by analogy. Since the term "Sūtra" (the text) is formed by incorporating the expressed meaning (*vācya*) as its specific name, here too, the term "Commentary" (*ṭīkā*) is formed by incorporating the explained meaning (*vācya*) as its specific designation.

One thus understands that this commentary does not merely explain another sūtra. Among the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-vigraha*), it is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative).
"Commentary" (*śu*) means to unravel (*śu*) and to provide a key (*kai*). It refers to unraveling and providing a key to the words and meanings so that they are free from obstruction. Furthermore...

The term "Preface" (xu) refers to using the title of the commentary to simultaneously indicate the preface; it is so designated for the sake of brevity, and the annotation is provided to clarify this.
It describes the essential tenets of this sutra as well as the reasons for composing the commentary.
Regarding the two records that commemorate him: Chongguo marked the location upon which he relied, namely the state of Baziguo in the Han dynasty;
later, because its customs and resources flourished, it was named after him. This is present-day Guozhou. The śramaṇa Zongmi cites the person who relies [on the teaching]:
in Sanskrit, *śramaṇa* means "diligent and quiescent," referring to one who diligently practices what is good and ceases from what is evil—such a person is a son of the Śākya.
This is a general designation. Zongmi was the name of the commentator; his secular surname was He.

He was born in the first year of the Jianzhong era of the Tang dynasty and passed away on the sixth day of the first month in the first year of the Huichang era. Emperor Xuanzong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Dinghui.
While living, he resided at Mount Guifeng in Zhongnan, and people have continued to refer to him as Guifeng to this day. [The interlocutor] asks about the origin of the commentator’s name.
Residing at Mount Guifeng, Yanbiao wrote "Chongguo Danyiti" (Answering a Single Topic Regarding Chongguo) in two parts, clarifying both points: first, because it is the homeland of one's parents;
second, because it is the place where the *śāstra* was composed. Regarding the first point, by not forgetting one's origin, the way of filial piety is made manifest.

Regarding the second, by highlighting that the composition was produced there, the record of the event is established. A "narrator" (*shu*) reveals the function of a person, whereas an "author" (*zuo*) [establishes the work itself].
It says: "The 'Exposition by the Sage' refers to the fact that Master Mingyi Jing and others have previously provided commentaries and explanations;

There are six phrases. The first two clarify the vertical profundity of filial piety; the next two demonstrate the horizontal breadth of filial conduct;

and in the final two phrases, the first reveals that the two teachings share the same fundamental source, while the last clarifies the universal application and concludes by pointing to the vertical profundity.

Regarding the term "chaotic" (*hundun*) within the section on vertical profundity: it refers to the pure primordial qi, both clear and turbid, prior to the differentiation of yin and yang, heaven and earth.

Because they are in harmony with one another, it is called *hundun* (the undifferentiated chaos), also known as *hunyuan* (the primordial source). As the *Daodejing* states: "There was something formed in its totality, born before heaven and earth.
And as the *Yijing* states: "The Great Ultimate (*taiji*) gives rise to the two polarities (*liangyi*). This is precisely what the non-Buddhist teachings of this region describe:

that humans, animals, and all else are generated and nurtured by the void and the Great Way (*daodao*). They claim that the Way follows its own nature (*ziran*) and is produced from the primal qi (*yuanqi*), and that the primal qi...

Heaven and earth give birth to all things, and heaven and earth give birth to the myriad creatures; therefore, whether one is foolish or wise, noble or humble, poor or wealthy, suffering or happy, all are simply received from time and fate.
Their death and life, their transformations and changes, ultimately return to the One Qi (the single vital energy). The *Baihutong* says:

"In the beginning of heaven and earth, first there was the Great Commencement (*Taichu*), followed by the Great Beginning (*Taishi*); once the signs of form had emerged, it was named the Great [One]."
Originally, the primordial chaos was continuous; it could not be seen and could not be heard. Only then did it undergo differentiation, and the clear and the turbid were separated.
The essence emerged, its radiance spread, and it measured things and bestowed life—this is the ultimate discourse on the original beginning.

Now, regarding what is discussed in the inner teachings, let us first examine it according to the Hīnayāna: it is said that all sentient beings establish [their existence] through the six consciousnesses and the three poisons.
The receptacle world undergoes a cycle of four phases—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—each lasting twenty *kalpas*. From the beginning of the *kalpa* of emptiness, the world is formed.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "In the realm of emptiness, a great wind arises; its breadth is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen *lakṣas*.

Nothing, not even a diamond, can destroy it. This is called the Wind that Sustains the World. The clouds of the Light-Sound (*Ābhāsvara*) and Diamond-Treasury (*Vajragarbha*) spread throughout the three thousandfold world-system."
The rain from the realms is as large as axle-trees; a great wind checks it so that it does not flow, yet it falls to a depth of sixteen *lakṣas*.
First, the sequence of the Vajradhātu is established; a vajra-cloud pours down rain that fills its interior. First, the realm of Brahmā is formed, and so on up to the Yāma heaven.
The wind stirs the ocean waters to form Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, and so forth. The turbid dregs become the mountain-lands, the four continents, and the mud.

Beyond the salt ocean and the Cakravāḍa mountains lies the realm of vessels (*bhājana-loka*). Its formation lasts for one *kalpa* of increase and decrease, extending even up to the Second Dhyāna heaven.

When their merit is exhausted, beings descend to be born among humans. Initially, they consume earth-cakes and forest creepers; later, they eat non-glutinous rice, which they cannot digest, leading to the emergence of excrement and urine, as well as the differentiation of male and female forms.
They then divide the fields and establish masters, who in turn seek ministers and assistants, resulting in all manner of social distinctions. (19)
The twenty increases and decreases combined with the preceding [periods] constitute what is called the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*).

The commentary states: "The great wind of the empty realm is precisely that primordial chaotic *qi*; thus we know that this chaos is the beginning of this kalpa of formation. At this time, the way of filial piety was already latent within it; it is not something that began only now, which is why it is said to "begin with" filial piety.

The *Jingshou shenqi* states: "When the primal qi was in a state of chaos (*hundun*), filial piety was contained therein. Question: Now, when Buddhist scriptures instead rely on worldly teachings to speak of "chaos," what is the reason for this?
Answer: Practicing filial piety to repay one's parents is precisely intended to guide the common people.

Furthermore, since these teachings are established upon returning to one's hometown so that both monastics and laypeople may hear them together, if one were to point specifically to the beginning of the kalpa, the common folk would find it difficult to understand.

Furthermore, when "Chun-hun" (the primordial chaos) is designated, the fourfold assembly understands it; as for the distinctions between the two teachings clarified below, many citations from Confucian texts are intended to convey this same meaning.
That which "blocks" heaven and earth—"Heaven" (*tian*)—is spoken of as "stabilizing" (*zhen*); situated above and governing what is below, it serves as the stabilizer for humanity.
"Earth" (*di*) means "change" (*yi*); it refers to the generation and nourishment of the myriad things, its capacity to harbor and sustain, and its nature of exchange, transformation, and change.
Since filial piety begins with the primordial chaos (*hundun*), it arises simultaneously with Heaven and Earth and fills the space between them.
Thus, the *Liji*, in the "Jiyi" chapter, quotes Zengzi as saying: "As for filial piety, if it is established, it fills Heaven and Earth; if it is spread, it extends across the four seas;
if it is bestowed upon posterity, it knows neither morning nor evening. Although these two sentences originate from different sources, [they convey the same truth].

The Master of the Commentary (*Sū-zhǔ*) employs these [terms] together to establish a single meaning: the preceding phrase clarifies the fundamental origin of filiality, hence it says, "it begins with primordial chaos" (*hùnzhùn*);
the subsequent phrase reveals the manifestation of filiality in form, hence it says, "it fills heaven and earth. Thus, the meaning of vertical depth is made manifest.
The former masters merely applied a one-sided allocation, holding that the first phrase is vertical while the second phrase is horizontal.
Now, based on the new commentary, there appears to be a coherent thread following the intention of the *Fuhui shuzhu* (the Commentary Master’s Harmonization of Texts).

However, while both [interpretations] accord with reason, the choice between them depends on the individual; this is precisely what the ancients warned against. As for that which manifests the horizontal breadth and vertical penetration through which humans and spirits pass:
although the text mentions humans and spirits specifically, it actually encompasses all six realms of existence; indeed, all living beings without exception are included.

There are parents, old friends, and spirits; all take the Way of Filial Piety as essential. Furthermore, while a person may practice filial piety toward others, they can also move the divine principle.
Although there are these two perspectives, the former explanation is superior. As for "pervading the noble and the mean," the two terms "noble" and "mean" encompass the five ranks:
first, the Son of Heaven; second, the feudal lords; third, the high ministers and great officers; fourth, the scholars; and fifth, the common people.
Among humans, the Son of Heaven alone is noble; when he is base, he is but a commoner. The three intermediate ranks communicate between nobility and baseness.
Although the *Xiaojing* explains filial piety in five chapters, each clarifying its specific application, the source of all hundredfold practices does not differ.
Therefore, from the Son of Heaven down to the commoner, there has never been one who practiced filial piety without beginning or end and yet suffered from its failure to reach fulfillment.

"One dies only after [one's task] is finished; therefore, there is no beginning or end. There has never been a case where one’s strength was insufficient yet one allowed the practice not to proceed; thus, from the Son of Heaven above down to the common people below, all must have both an end and a beginning.

One does not speak of 'beginning and end' while looking at the 'end and beginning'—it is because one must be as cautious at the end as at the beginning. Only by having an end can one perfect the goodness of the beginning; if one cannot complete the end, then even if the beginning was attained, it will inevitably be lost.

Earth is limited because it exists only within one’s own physical form; next, the human spirit (*shen*) is narrower still, as it is a constituent of the two polarities (*yi*);

when heaven and earth were separated, the two polarities had already divided, and thus it became relatively broad. The penetration of the human spirit, however, is due to the filial piety of the heart.
Since this has been clearly manifested, it further broadly encompasses both the noble and the humble; thus, the Way of relying on reverence is doubly emphasized.

Regarding "the sorrow for the frost," the *Jiyi* (Meaning of Sacrifices) states: "When the autumn frost and dew have descended, the gentleman treading upon them must feel a sense of melancholy;

this is not because of their coldness. When the spring rain and dew have moistened [the earth], the gentleman treading upon them must feel a sense of trepidation, as if he were about to see [his ancestors] again.
Now, the meaning of the *Shu* (Commentary) clarifies that filial thought is uninterrupted; whether moving or stationary, his heart is as keen as if he were treading upon them.
Because the characters for "snow" and "frost" are easily mistaken for those for "dew," it is said that one encounters them at every step.

The *Liji*, *Tangong* chapter, states: "The gentleman has a sorrow that lasts a lifetime. Former scholars annotated this, saying: "It refers to his constant remembrance of his parents. Is this not precisely what is meant? Regarding the "sorrow of wind and tree," the *Kongzi Jiayu* says:
When Confucius was traveling to Qi, he heard the sound of someone working on wood along the way; the tone of the sound was profoundly mournful.
Confucius said to his charioteer, "This weeping is indeed sorrowful, yet it is not the sorrow of one who has lost a parent.
He urged the driver forward, and after proceeding a short distance, they saw a strange man holding a sickle and wearing a rope belt, weeping without any sign of grief.
Confucius descended from his carriage, pursued him, and asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Wuqiu Wuzi. Confucius said, "Are you not now—"
"What is the cause of this sorrowful wailing at the funeral? Qiu Wuzi replied, "I have three failures;
I realized them only late in life—what use is regret now? He asked, "May I hear of these three failures? I hope you will not conceal anything from me.
Qiu Wuzi said, "In my youth, I loved learning and traveled throughout the world, but upon my return, I had lost my parents—this was my first failure. When I grew older..."
Serving the Lord of Qi, he found the ruler arrogant and extravagant, losing his retainers and failing to fulfill his ministerial duties; this was the second failure.
His lifelong close friends have now all parted from him; this is the third failure. Indeed, a tree desires stillness, yet the wind does not cease;
a son desires to nourish his parents, yet they do not wait. That which has passed and will not return is time; that which can never be seen again is one’s parents. I beg leave to follow them.
This disciple then threw himself into the water and died. Confucius said, "Young man, take note of this; it shall serve as a sufficient warning.

From that time on, thirteen disciples took their leave to return home to care for their parents. This account merely extracts and employs that text to illustrate how when matters and the heart diverge, one laments and regrets it for a lifetime;
hence the words, "I hold this in my heart forever."
Second, explaining the mindfulness of wishing for recompense, in two parts: first, the reason for searching the scriptures; second, first, showing reliance on Confucianism.

[The text] uses the two characters "qiè yǐ" (privately and thus) to indicate the mind capable of reflection, meaning that one privately reflects upon those matters. The four phrases beginning with "zhōngshēn" (throughout one's life) cite the matters being reflected upon;
"zhōngshēn" and "zúshì" (the end of one’s life) alternate in their phrasing. Regarding "fénlǒng" (tomb mounds), the *Tángōng* states: "In antiquity, there were tombs..."
"But I shall not raise a mound over it, for I, Qiu, am a man of the east, west, south, and north; it would be improper not to mark my resting place. Thereupon he raised a mound four chi high.
Regarding the practice of "bending the body" (curving the path) when visiting a grave: one does not ascend the mound. Zheng Xuan’s commentary states:

"Mound" (lǒng) refers to the tomb; "grave" (mù) refers to the surrounding precinct. A filial Confucian, after the death of his parents, carries earth on his back to form a mound and plants cypress trees in rows.

Lumù served for three years to exhaust his filial sincerity; "Zhēng" and "Cháng" are names for ancestral sacrifices. The *Jìtǒng* (The System of Sacrifices) in the *Líjì* states: "In all sacrifices there are four seasons:
in spring it is called *yào*, in summer it is called *dí*, in autumn it is called *cháng*, and in winter it is called *zhēng*.

Here, I have briefly cited only autumn and winter, just as the *Xiàojīng* says, "Sacrificing in spring and autumn, one thinks of them according to the season," which encompasses both summer and winter. Thus it is.
According to Confucian rites, one dwells in a hut by the grave for three years and performs seasonal sacrifices, yet these do not necessarily last a lifetime;
now, by citing long-term practices to illustrate short-term ones, you merely demonstrate their lack of benefit.

Although matters such as "unfolding" [the mourning period] involve both inclusion and exclusion—wherein the former two points may be granted as a matter of personal conscience, yet their removal does not assist the deceased on the path to the netherworld—I have thus extracted the essence of this matter and set it aside.
I did not explain this to the ignorant; my current deletion of it is because the characters "su" (遂) and "zi" (字) are terms that signify two matters being carried out simultaneously.

Second, clarifying the interpretation from the commentary: first, seeking the Dharma according to one's aspirations. There are six phrases in the text; the first two phrases clarify the seeking of the Dharma.

The latter four lines clarify the intent behind the initial seeking of the Dharma; therein, the term "thereupon" (*suì*) serves as a phrase that connects the preceding with the subsequent, indicating that both matters were practiced concurrently.

Having realized that such acts as dwelling in a tomb or performing ancestral sacrifices are insufficient to assist the spiritual consciousness in its transcendence, one consequently searches for and investigates the scriptural teachings of the sages and worthies within the Tripiṭaka (noting that while those equal to the Buddha are called "Sages," all others are termed "Worthies"—even those on the stage of Equal Enlightenment are still called "Samantabhadra"). Furthermore, regarding the Three... [text continues].

Within the Tripiṭaka, the Vinaya consists solely of what was ordained by the Buddha, whereas the Sūtras and Śāstras include teachings spoken for disciples and others; thus, among the disciples there were likewise sages and worthies—on the great scale, the Ten Sages and Three Worthies; on the small scale, the Seven Sages and Seven Worthies.

[This text] sets forth the methods for reverently seeking, pursuing cultivation, and offering posthumous rites for them. Question: Since the teachings of the sages and worthies are nothing other than those intended to benefit sentient beings, why is it necessary to further search for and reverently seek them?

Answer: It is exactly as you have asked. Furthermore, among the myriad varieties of medical prescriptions, one must select those that are appropriate to the specific ailment. Thus, although the Dharma is universally beneficial, one must diligently seek out those specific teachings that correspond to the particular needs of the deceased. Therefore, one must respectfully investigate and pursue these methods.

The commentary treats this by weighing it against the minds of those for whom it is intended; thus, one must search [the text]. Later, the first two lines of the "Holding in Mind" section praise the profundity of its merit.
Although this sutra is included within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, its extraction from suffering and its provision for kinsmen constitute its most essential core.

Even a single day’s offering of a basin can rescue the extreme sufferings of the three evil realms; such a minute capacity can bring about vast benefit, and even a small virtue can shatter [great obstacles].

If such a great evil as this is practiced, how could it not be considered non-sublime? Since it should respond with sincerity and accord with one's heart, the latter two phrases demonstrate the mode of practice;
they summarize the subsequent scriptural text to clarify the timing of the event. The Sūtra says:

The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the Saṃgha of the ten directions observes the *pravāraṇā*, you should, for the sake of your parents of seven generations past and those of the present..."

Regarding those who are in distress and hardship among their parents, one provides food of a hundred flavors, the five fruits, vessels for drawing and pouring water, fragrant oil, upright candles, beds, mats, and bedding—all the sweet and delicious things of the world—placed within these vessels.
As explained in detail below in the commentary, the phrase "providing food and so forth" refers to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*);
since sound alone is missing from among them, it is established as four matters based on the other four sense-objects (*catvāra āyatanāni*). Some say: [text continues].
The four requisites—lodgings, clothing, food, and medicinal decoctions—are detailed here without difference from the aforementioned traditional meanings;

indeed, these have already been fully established. Alas! Those at Mount Gu were confused by the later commentaries and, conversely, claimed that this interpretation suffers from the fault of being overly diffuse.
The "Three Honored Ones" (Sanzun) refers directly to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, so called because they are revered and esteemed by the world.
Second, regarding the practice based on the sūtras, there are four phrases in the explanation of the text. The first two phrases clarify the making of offerings;

the latter two phrases demonstrate that the cultivation and honoring [of the Dharma] rests with oneself, which constitutes the practice of self-benefit (*svārtha*), while explaining and revealing what has not yet been heard constitutes the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha*). As for "honor" (*chóng*), it means to revere.

As for "year" (*zài*), the *Erya* (Explanations of the Elegant) in its section on Heaven states: "A year is called *zài*. In the eras of Tang and Yu it was called *zài*; in the Xia it was called *suì*; in the Shang it was called..."
Regarding the term *niàn* (year) used for the Zhou dynasty, Li Xun stated: "Each [dynasty] records its own events to show that they do not follow one another. Sun Yan stated:

"'Suì' (suǐ) takes its name from the *suìxīng* (the Sieve Star) completing one revolution; 'sì' (sì) takes its name from the completion of the seasonal sacrifices; 'niàn' (niàn) takes its name from the single ripening of the year's grain;

and 'zǎi' (zǎi) takes its name from the end of things and the beginning of anew. This refers to the master himself saying that he has obtained this scripture year after year, and that the monks perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination/invitation) annually.
Ri has been practicing and establishing this based upon it for many years already. Regarding the term "jiang" (講), the *Shuowen* states it means "to reconcile.
"Gao" (誥) refers to the Buddha’s edict, which is precisely this sutra. "Gao" is also written as "gao" (告). Liu Xi’s *Shiming* says: "The superior’s command to the subordinate is called 'gao';

'gao' means 'to awaken,' so that [the recipient] awakens and understands the intention of the [superior]. This is like the *Dagao* (Great Edict) in the *Shangshu* and other such Buddhist scriptures. Since the Buddhist scriptures...
This is because it awakens sentient beings so that they may understand the Buddha’s intention; thus it is called "instruction" (*kathā*) to reveal what has not yet been heard.
Now, the Confucians take natural affection as filial piety (*xiao*) and the extension of love to all things as benevolence (*ren*).

By now revealing this to them so that they may hear it and practice it accordingly to repay their parents' kindness, one follows the path of extending love to all things—the great compassionate practice of a Bodhisattva.
This is why, whenever such an occasion arises, he cultivates and expounds the teachings, desiring to provide a basis for future generations to emulate him.

Second, the reasons for composing the commentary. First, the causes for the assembly and the resulting invitation; this passage contains six phrases. The first two phrases clarify the return to his home province to initiate the assembly:
namely, in the second year of the Dàhé era of Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty, he was summoned to the inner palace to consult on the essentials of the Dharma. Following this...
He requested to return to the mountains (intending to go back to Zhongnan). Later, at the request of the assembly, he entered Shu to establish a stele inscription for his former master.

Consequently, upon returning to his hometown, it happened to be the end of summer; therefore, he established the schedule based on the days of the month. "Kai" refers to lecturing on the sutras, while "she" refers to performing offerings. The following two lines indicate the characteristics of the two assemblies:
"monastics and laypeople" encompasses both the clergy and the laity, while "elders" includes all four groups [of disciples]. The *Book of Rites* states that those aged fifty...
It is said that "Ai" refers to assuming official duties, meaning one at the age of fifty who is capable of serving as a Great Officer and managing affairs independently.
At sixty, one is called "Qi," meaning one who directs others; at this stage of "ear-harmony," one is no longer fit to handle administrative tasks but merely points out matters and employs others.
The *Erya* states: "Qi, Ai, and Die all mean 'old. Therefore, these terms are now commonly used as designations for elders. One should follow and practice [these teachings] with both sorrow and joy.

Upon hearing that the lecture was being opened, his heart gave rise to both sorrow and joy; seeing that the ritual vessels had been prepared, he resolved with a joyful aspiration to follow and practice them.

Within this, the sorrow and joy do not exceed three pairs: sorrow because he heard of the profound weight of his parents' kindness; joy because he obtained the supreme Dharma as a recompense; and sorrow because in the past he had not heard it, while joy arises from hearing it now.
Furthermore, there is sorrow because others have not yet heard it, and joy because he himself has now attained it. The latter two phrases clarify these points.

I have composed this commentary because the petitions [for such works] have not been uniform; thus it is said they were "requested with different mouths. Yet, as there was no difference in the sound [of their request], it is said they were "in unison.
Because it is a new commentary in contrast to those written by the ancients, it is called the *Xinshu* (New Commentary), as indicated by the citations from the Tripitaka Master and others below.

Now, why should the present be established at the expense of the ancient? It is certainly not for nothing: perhaps the former were too prolix or too terse, or perhaps their doctrines and methods diverged from the path. This is intended to ensure that [the teaching] is truly...
Fu Zhengli’s profound admiration for this work is perfectly suited to his own disposition and sincere devotion; thus, he makes this request.

Regarding the second point, "cherishing one's parents" (*huai qin*) and "being true to one's feelings" (*yun qing*), there are four phrases: the first two phrases demonstrate cherishing one's parents, while the latter two clarify being true to one's feelings.
The mention of "pine and cypress" refers to the trees planted at a grave mound; by pointing to these objects, it expresses the subject—the parents—and thereby articulates the essence of filial piety.

[The text] also [includes Wen Jia’s statement]: "The tomb of the Son of Heaven is three *zhen* high and planted with pines; that of the feudal lords is half that height and planted with cypresses; that of the Great Officers is eight feet and planted with *luan* trees; that of the scholars is four feet and planted with paulownias; commoners have no mounds and plant willows and poplars.

During the Han dynasty there was no fixed regulation, and pine and cypress were planted universally. The gates established in the villages and neighborhoods are those set up at the entrances of the wards;

they are erected as a means to summon the elders, thereby manifesting respect. Having already cherished one's parents, one respects the aged and venerable; thus, in accordance with this sincere sentiment, the memorial tablet (*shu*) is prepared.

"Yeshi" (Also thus) signifies respectful and sincere compliance. "Laqing" (Coming of feelings) refers to the earnest sincerity initiated by those who are aged and venerable, manifesting as reverent action.
This means that through this simple and plain [offering], one practices the essential and subtle Way of filial piety.
The second part, the commentary on the text, has two sections. First, regarding the homage and request for protection at the beginning of various treatises and commentaries:

it is clarified that one may perform a full homage to the Triple Gem (as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-mahāṭīkā*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-ṭīkā*, etc.); or one may proceed directly without a formal homage (as in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* and the *Laghu-vivaraṇa on the Awakening of Faith*, etc.);

or one may pay homage solely to the Buddha-gem (as in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, etc.); or one may pay homage only to the Dharma-gem (as in the *Dharmadhātu-aviśeṣa-śāstra*, etc.). Thus, there are diverse paths according to the extent of the text.

The methods of composition vary and their stylistic forms are manifold; they cannot be standardized by a single rule. In this present verse, some instances involve taking refuge in the Buddha Jewel alone, which can be understood from the text itself;
others involve taking refuge in all Three Jewels, which likewise does not contradict the meaning. This is because the Dharma is the word of the Buddha and the Saṃgha are the sons of the Buddha;
thus, by mentioning the person (the Buddha), one encompasses his words (the Dharma), and by clarifying the father (the Buddha), one includes his children (the Saṃgha).
The former masters’ interpretation assigns these three verses to the Three Jewels respectively: the first verse’s meaning of taking refuge in the Buddha is clear;
the second verse expounds the sūtras as the Jewel of the Dharma; and the third verse concerns the assembly of noble ones, which is the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

I have repeatedly examined the text in detail from beginning to end, and find that while the narrative describes the sequence of events, it is certainly not exclusively concerned with [the Three Jewels] alone.

Regarding the Three Jewels, what is now discussed concerns their acceptance and rejection based on the initial verse; although that verse formally takes refuge in the Buddha, its meaning also encompasses all three, and thus it is not restricted to one alone.

Generally, when discussing the Three Jewels, there are three distinctions: the provisional manifestation (*saṃniśrita*), the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the identical essence (*tattva*).
As these are explained extensively in other chapters, they are not cited here to avoid prolixity. For the time being, I shall clarify them by focusing primarily on the distinct characteristics.
The three verses are divided into four meanings: first, paying homage; second, praising the object of refuge; third, requesting secret empowerment; and fourth, making vows before returning home.
Since one must first perform the rites of propriety when approaching the Most Honorable One, the initial section is the paying of homage.

Once the cultivation of reverence is complete, there follows the praise of virtues. Since such virtues necessarily possess the capacity for altruism, they can surely bestow secret empowerment upon me.
Therefore, there is a third [type of prostration] which requests the Buddha’s secret empowerment; because the intention is to benefit both [self and others], there is a fourth.

Regarding the initial "kowtow" (稽首), this refers to the ritual of reverence by which one touches the head to the ground. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (智度論) clarifies that there are three methods of salutation: first, the oral salutation (which is a greeting and is called the "lower salutation");

second, bending the knees with the head not touching the ground (which is kneeling and is called the "middle salutation"); and third, touching the head to the ground (which is the present-day kowtow and is called the "upper salutation").

Among the three types of ritual (*li*), this is the most supreme; it is the ultimate expression of humility and reverence, and nothing exceeds it. Within the three modes of action (*trikarma*), one first employs the physical gesture (*kāyakarman*);

next, one praises that which is taken as refuge, which necessarily involves the vocal action (*vākkarman*); and finally, one requests the bestowal of vows, which pertains to the mental action (*manaskarman*).
Thus, the three modes of action are complete. This is done to manifest that the Buddha possesses the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds, thereby perfecting these three.
Because his karma is virtuous and because he has accomplished the causes for the three wheels.
Second, praising that to which he has returned. This has two parts: first, praising the perfection of the path of his own practice;

second, first, citing the realms of transformation—the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, together with the great trichiliocosm, which is the realm transformed by Śākyamuni. Since there are those to be transformed...
The realm necessarily includes the person who transforms; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "This triple world is now all mine;

this dilapidated old house belongs to one person," and thus it is called the "master. Because the object of transformation is cited to indicate the subject who transforms, the heading is titled "The Sphere of Transformation.

Second, the narrative of virtues and conduct has two parts: first, the simultaneous indication of cause and fruit. The first two characters indicate causal practice, and the following three characters indicate [the fruit].

Although the fruits of practice and conduct differ in ten thousand ways, filial piety (*xiao*) serves as the comprehensive principle that encompasses them all; although virtues are immeasurable, they are collectively subsumed under the clan name.
The two characters "Śākya" are specifically applied to the Teacher of the World. This is translated as "Able Benevolence" (*Néngrén*). The *Śāsanānusaṃsā-śāstra* states:

"Because he manifests skillful means to transform sentient beings, and because he further demonstrates the nobility of his family and clan, 'Great Filial Piety' and 'Nobility' apply universally to all Buddhas and are fully possessed by them."

The addition of the two characters "Muni" (translated here as "Silent One") is because the *Lun* (Treatise) states that this represents the merits of all Buddhas and further demonstrates the purity of their own essence.
Because they are silent, they do not abide in saṃsāra; because they are capable sages, they do not abide in nirvāṇa.

As compassion and wisdom operate in tandem, this auspicious title was established. In the *Zuanyao* (Compendium of Essentials), the expression of homage specifically mentions only "Muni," each following its respective scripture.
The fundamental principle is likewise not at variance [with this].
The second pair explains cause and effect: the upper phrase indicates causal practice, which explains the meaning of "supreme filial piety";

the lower phrase manifests resultant virtue, which explains the "World-Honored One Śākyamuni. "Accumulated kalpas" refers to the vast duration of time, namely the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

Regarding the repayment of parental kindness, there is both a general and a specific sense. The general sense refers to the long-term cultivation of the six perfections, all of which constitute repaying kindness.

The specific sense refers to serving one’s parents wherever one may be, being able to fulfill filial piety in every circumstance. As for attaining enlightenment, one first delivers one’s compassionate parents;

beginning with preaching the Dharma to Queen Māyā after her ascent to heaven, and ending with personally carrying King Śuddhodana’s coffin to his funeral, such is the repayment of kindness—its scope is vast indeed.
When one practices filial piety in this manner, that filiality is truly great. By accumulating causes, one ascends to the higher realms;

through the accumulation of merit over kalpas, one repays the kindness of parents and attains perfect enlightenment—this signifies the fulfillment of the present fruit, for the practice of the six pāramitās and the deeds of repaying one's parents over successive kalpas have all been brought to completion.
Thus, he was born above in Tuṣita Heaven and descended to Jambudvīpa, where he did not inherit the royal throne, but renounced his kin and departed from his kingdom.
This is said because, from sitting beneath the tree until the thirty-four moments of mind, the fetters were severed and the fruit of the fivefold dharma-body was perfected.
This is precisely to distinguish [this] from false awakening; as the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Because one awakens to and knows both worldly and supramundane dharmas.

Second, praising the benefit of others by expounding the Dharma. Part one clarifies the arousal of compassion and the subsequent exposition: the preceding phrase indicates the arousal of compassion, while the following phrase...

"Manifesting" (*ming*) refers to the intention to perform; as the *Shijing* says, "Just beginning the ten-thousand dances," it signifies perpetuity. "Bestowing" (*xi*) refers to granting gifts; as the *Shijing* says, "The filial son is never exhausted;

he shall forever bestow upon you his kindred. The Master [Zhu] borrows the force of these expressions to apply them here. The term "all classes" (*zhong lei*) serves as a general designation for all living beings:
in the case of the filial son, it means distancing himself from evil and transforming toward goodness; in the case of the two parents, it means departing from suffering and attaining joy.

All who participate among the ranks of humanity receive its bounty. As the Sūtra says: "For those disciples of the Buddha who cultivate filial piety and obedience, it causes all hardships to be free from sorrow and suffering.
Is this not precisely what that refers to? Furthermore, the words established by the Supreme Sage do not issue forth without a cause;
they respond to the request of Maudgalyāyana and thus expound this gateway of repaying one's parents. This is what was meant in the preceding preface regarding responding to the filial son.
This is indeed the essence of such sincere devotion.
Second, regarding the manifestation of the capacity for altruism: those who betray the kindness of others are generally referred to as the ungrateful and unfilial among worldly people;

if one must always seek to repay a debt of gratitude owed to another, how much more so for the labor and toil of one’s parents in giving birth and raising one? In the Confucian tradition, this is expressed as establishing one's character and bringing honor to one's name.

To explain the term "filial" (*xunse chengzhi*) as it is defined here: it refers to those who cultivate the mind, uphold the precepts, preach the Dharma, and benefit sentient beings—such as these are true filial sons.
If one does not act in this way, they are all ungrateful. Now, among all sentient beings in the world, those who practice filial piety are few, while those who are ungrateful are many;
this is simply because, from time immemorial, ignorance has caused them to delude the truth and cling to forgetfulness, having already rooted themselves [in error].

Because the root is inverted, the branches and twigs are all ablaze. The Great Sage, wishing to cause beings to turn back from delusion and return to the truth, established his transformative teachings through gradual stages.
Is it not precisely this sutra that serves to reverse this evil ingratitude and bring about the goodness of repaying virtue?
Therefore, the subsequent phrase says: "All are able to recompense that which is boundless. The expression "boundless" (*wǎngjí*) originates from the *Mao Shi*, as mentioned above.
The preceding has already been cited.

"Three requests" refers to the invocation for divine assistance; the upper phrase expresses the intention, while the lower phrase seeks empowerment. "I" refers to the Master himself (the author of the commentary), employing the conventional designations of "guest" and "host" according to worldly custom.
"Praise" (*zàn*) means to assist and bring to completion the Holy Teaching; it refers to his aspiration. "Narration" (*shù*) means to transmit.

The ancient practice of not explicitly naming [the specific deity] was intended to demonstrate humility. To begin with, although the initial expression of homage specifically refers only to the Buddha Śākyamuni, this current prayer for secret empowerment is offered universally to all the sages.
It is not limited to the Buddhas alone, but encompasses the entirety of the Three Vehicles; thus, through their mutual and implicit manifestation, it truly accords with the inclusion of all.

Furthermore, when the sacred majesty bestows its influence upon beings, it does so both manifestly and secretly. Manifestly, there is the touching of the crown and the praise of one's virtues; secretly, there is...
Because he was secretly imbued with spiritual power and did not dare to seek a manifest response, he now simply requests hidden assistance;

this is precisely the intention behind what the various bodhisattvas in the *Lotus Sūtra* said: "We only pray that the World-Honored One, remaining in other lands, will behold us from afar and provide protection.

Fourth, regarding the making of vows: the preceding phrase cites the person who makes the vow, while the subsequent phrase clarifies the matter for which the vow is made—namely, the application of the bodhisattva’s [power].
Because the mind does not strive for its own exclusive benefit, it creates this benefit for both oneself and others;
those who survive are freed from the sufferings of illness, affliction, and distress, and attain the joys of tranquility and delight. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"May our present parents live for a hundred years, free from disease and all the calamities of suffering. Regarding the deceased, there are two intentions, the first of which accords with the scriptural text and is free [from worldly attachment].

Because those in the three miserable realms obtain the bliss of humans and devas, the Sūtra says: "I vow that my parents of seven generations shall leave the suffering of hungry ghosts and be born among humans and devas, where their merit and bliss are limitless.

Second, according to the Master of the Commentary, based on the Buddha’s original intent, this means causing them to leave behind the sufferings of both *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) death, and to attain the bliss of Great Bodhi and Nirvāṇa. Leaving suffering behind is precisely the function of Great Compassion.
"Joy" (*sukha*) is the achievement of Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*); "Constant Joy" (*nitya-sukha*) is one of the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*), and it is also where the esoteric meaning resides.

[The section on] the two introductory chapters and the formal explanation has four parts: first, the opening of the chapter; second, the formal explanation. Within the first part (the opening of the chapter), there are four sections:
first, identifying the origin; second, determining its affiliation; third, indicating its veneration; and fourth, explaining its characteristics. These are the four categories.

Regarding the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), it should be understood that the first three sūtras are explained through their underlying meaning, while the final one is analyzed according to the literal text.
Second, the actual explanation has four parts: first, the causes for the arising of the teaching; second, the initial listing of the chapters.

Second, the detailed explanation of the four [sections]. First, regarding the response to past causes: first, the topical outline; second, the actual exposition. Regarding the first, the response concerning the causes for his own practice:
*Siddhārtha*—here translated as "All Meanings Accomplished"—was the legitimate heir to King Śuddhodana, and thus was named "Crown Prince.

Yet, he did not succeed to the royal throne, but instead grew weary of worldly glory. "Abandoning kin and leaving the state" means he departed from his father the king and others, crossing... [the Ganges].
Entering the mountains from the city refers to his practice; "practicing" means that after six years of asceticism, he attained the Way. Under the tree, he severed the fetters;

The ancestral temple (*zongmiao*) is established to clarify the transmission between family and state; the distinction between family and state is made by the relative narrowness or breadth of their boundaries.
The "state" refers to the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords (*zhuhou*); the "family" refers to the high ministers, great officers, and ordinary officers or commoners who lack a temple.

Furthermore, it is restricted to four persons. *Zong* signifies honor; *miao* signifies appearance. This means honoring one's ancestors and patriarchs, preserving their physical likeness, and performing solemn sacrificial rites. (From the *Liji*, "Jieshi")

When the Dharma-cloud covers the world, there is a sovereign who divides the land to establish states (the division of the Nine Provinces' lands constitutes the fiefdoms of the feudal lords), establishes capitals and founds towns (establishing the capitals for the high ministers and founding the towns for the Great Officers and scholars;

this refers to the royal domain and the territories within the states of the various lords). He establishes ancestral temples, *tiào* shrines, altars, and mounds to perform sacrifices, thereby determining the degrees of kinship and the scale of offerings.

Therefore, the sovereign establishes seven temples (four for close ancestors, one for the founding ancestor, and two *tiào* shrines for former kings, totaling seven), along with one altar and one mound.

The *shàn* (this is located outside the seven [ancestral temples]; a mound of earth is called a *tán*, while cleared ground is called a *shàn*; these are established for close relatives by mounding earth and for distant relatives by clearing the ground, signifying that they are about to depart). It is said: "The Temple of the *Kǎo*" (the temple of the father; *kǎo* means accomplished;

it refers to the father possessing the beauty of accomplished virtue). "The Temple of the *Wáng-kǎo*" (the temple of the grandfather; *wáng* means lord; this says the grandfather possesses the lordly virtue of accomplishment. Since the grandfather is more venerable than the father, the title of "lord" is added).

"The Temple of the *Huáng-kǎo*" (the temple of the great-grandfather; *huáng* means great; he is a lord. Since the great-grandfather is even more venerable, the designation of "great lord" is used). "The Temple of the *Xiǎn-kǎo*" (the temple of the high-grandfather; *xiǎn* means manifest; the high-grandfather resides in...).

The four ancestral temples are the most superior. They are called the Temples of the Patriarchal Ancestors (*zǔkǎo miào*); "patriarch" (*zǔ*) signifies the beginning, for this temple represents the origin of the King, hence it is called the Temple of the Patriarchal Ancestors.

All these are offered monthly sacrifices. The distant temples are designated as *tiāo*. There are two *tiāo* (the temples of Wén and Wǔ). Wén and Wǔ were both included in the category of those subject to relocation; however, because they were specially retained on account of their meritorious deeds, their temples are called *tiāo*.

The term *tiāo* means "to transcend," signifying that they have transcended upward [into a higher status]. Sacrifices of *xiǎng* and *cháng* (the seasonal sacrifices of the four times) cease [for them]; since Wén and Wǔ were specially retained, they do not receive monthly sacrifices. Beyond the *tiāo* temples are...

The *tán* (referring to the father of the High Ancestor) enshrines the *zhāo* lineages in the Wǔ-tiáo and the *mù* lineages in the Wén-tiáo; they do not receive seasonal sacrifices, but when there is a need for prayer, they are brought out to the *tán* to receive sacrifice.
Beyond the *tán* is the *shàn* (referring to the grandfather of the High Ancestor); he may not remain on the *tán*, and if there is a prayer, he is brought out to the *shàn* to receive sacrifice.

When there is a prayer at the *tán* or the *shàn*, one sacrifices; when there is no prayer, one ceases. Beyond the *shàn* is the realm of the *guǐ* (spirits). If someone from the *tán* is moved to the *shàn*, then those previously at the *shàn* are moved into the stone casket to become *guǐ*; even if there are prayers, they are no longer reached.

Only at the *di* and *xie* sacrifices do they emerge. The feudal lords established five temples, one altar (*tan*), and one cleared space (*shan*). These were called the temple of the father (*kao miao*), the temple of the grandfather (*wang kao miao*), and the temple of the great-grandfather (*huang kao miao*);

these all received monthly sacrifices. The temple of the great-great-grandfather (*xian kao miao*) and the temple of the high-great-grandfather (*zu kao miao*) ceased after the seasonal sacrifices of *xiang* and *chang*.

Once the high-great-grandfather was removed, an altar was established; once the altar was removed, a cleared space was established. Sacrifices were performed at the altar or the cleared space when there was a prayer; when there was no prayer, they ceased. Once the cleared space was removed, it became... [the text continues].

The Grand Officer of the Ghosts (Guǐ Dàfū) establishes three temples and two altars: the temple of the father (Kǎo Miào), the temple of the grandfather (Wáng Kǎo Miào), and the temple of the great-grandfather (Huáng Kǎo Miào).

Sacrifices of *xiǎng* and *cháng* are performed there, and that is all. For the "Manifest Father" (*Xiǎn Kǎo*) and the "Ancestral Father" (*Zǔ Kǎo*), there are no temples; when there is a prayer for them, an altar is erected and sacrifices are offered there.

Beyond the altar, they become ghosts (*guǐ*). An ordinary officer (*Shì*) of the direct line establishes two temples and one altar: the temple of the father and the temple of the grandfather. Sacrifices of *xiǎng* and *cháng* are performed there, and that is all. There is no temple for the great-grandfather.

When there was a prayer to be offered at the ancestral temple, an altar was constructed for the sacrifice; those removed from the altar were regarded as ghosts. For an *guan-shi* (official teacher), a single temple was called the *kao-miao* (temple of the father);

for one who had no temple for his *wang-kao* (grandfather), sacrifices were offered [at this level], and those removed from the *wang-kao* were regarded as ghosts. For common officers (*shu-shi*) and commoners (*shu-ren*), there were no temples; upon death, they were simply called ghosts.

(The *shi* refers to the *shi* of the direct line and the upper *shi*; the *guan-shi* is the middle *shi*; the *shu-shi* are the lower *shi*, including those of the rank of clerks and recorders. Thus, these rules are specifically restricted to the ancestral system of the Zhou house, which is why such textual evidence exists.

Regarding the two *tiāo* shrines of King Wu, the *Shangshu* states: "The ancestral temples of seven generations allow one to observe virtue. From this, we know that the ancestral temples serve as a universal standard;
this is the general outline. As for those who discuss the ritual of dispatching [the spirit] based on the *Wen* [Duke], there is no need for further detailed instruction here.

Furthermore, although the five [generations] below are generally summarized according to their conduct, the complete application is revealed by examining the prefaces of the classics, which state that despite the distinctions of high and low—
Although paths differ, the source of filial piety remains no different; among all deeds, when their major categories are enumerated, they all take filial piety as their foundation.

Part Two: Citing Examples to Fulfill the Middle Section. First, it demonstrates the meaning of being the foundation. Second, it provides a general summary to clarify the fundamental principle, which is filial piety itself.
The first chapter of this scripture elucidates the fundamental source of filial piety and clarifies the essential meaning of its practice;
therefore, it is given this title. "Supreme Virtue and Essential Way" refers directly to the practice of filial piety. As the Scripture says:

"The former kings possessed supreme virtue and an essential way by which they accorded with the world, so that the people lived in harmony and concord, and there was no resentment between those above and below. This arose because the virtue of filial piety is honored above all other deeds. (This refers to "supreme...")

Virtue. Filial piety subsumes the Five Constant Virtues (meaning it is the essential way); thus, Zhongni highlighted this to inform Zengzi, whereby the principle that the Confucian teaching takes filial piety as its foundation is made manifest.
Following "virtue," the text is divided: the first phrase indicates the root of practice, and the second phrase clarifies the root of instruction.
Furthermore, the main text of the first chapter states: "Now, filial piety is the root of virtue; it is the instruction..."

Regarding the phrase "that from which [the Way] arises," the commentary further adds the word "Way" because of the preceding text; its essence is the Root itself. Next, the section beginning with "How could there be...
clarifies that it must be practiced by humans. The initial passage is derived from the first chapter of the *Analects*:

"The gentleman applies himself to the root; when the root is established, the Way arises. Filiality and fraternal submission—these are the root of benevolence (*ren*). Benevolence is one of the Five Constant Virtues.

Furthermore, filial piety is established as its very foundation. Its principles are as fundamental as those of Heaven and Earth, as clearly revealed in the "Chapter on the Three Powers" of the *Classic of Filial Piety*:

"Filial piety is the constant principle of Heaven; it is the righteousness of Earth; it is the conduct of the people. It is the constant principle of Heaven and Earth, which the people take as their model.
"Constant" (*jing*) means enduring; "righteousness" (*yi*) means benefit. Heaven possesses the sun, moon, and stars, which illuminate all below.
It is the constant way of Heaven that the earth produces the hundred grains, grasses, and trees to provide for human use; this is what is called the natural benefit of the earth.
Since filial piety is both the constant way of Heaven and the natural benefit of the earth, those born between Heaven and Earth ought surely to model themselves after it and practice it.
Regarding the expressions "reaching upward" and "following downward," these appear in the *Tán Gōng*. Zéng Zǐ said to Zǐsī, "Jí, when I was holding my parents' [shoes]..."

In mourning, some do not take food or drink for seven days. Zisi said, "The former kings established the rites so that those who exceed them may bend down to reach them, and those who fall short may stand on tiptoe to attain them.

Therefore, when a gentleman observes the mourning for his parents, he does not take food or drink for three days, rising only after taking up the staff. (Zisi was the son of Boyu, the grandson of Confucius; his name was Ji and his courtesy name was Zisi. [End of citation]
To stand on one's heels is called *qi* (standing on tiptoe); ordinary people do not reach this height, so one must stand on tiptoe to reach it.

To stoop down to the head is called *fu* (bending down); the worthy can surpass others, so one must lower oneself to follow them. The ancient kings established the rites, valuing that which hits the mean:
if one is too close, one suppresses the worthy; if one is too distant, one neglects the unworthy. Thus, one knows that the Way of Filial Piety makes no such distinctions.
Although [the Master] spoke disparagingly of others later on, he could not abandon propriety; this is evident from the passage in the *Analects*, "Yang Huo," where Zai Wo asks:
"The three-year mourning period has been long enough. If a gentleman does not practice propriety for three years, propriety will surely decay;
if he does not practice music for three years, music will surely collapse. The old grain has perished and the new grain has risen; the fire-drills have been changed."
"When the three-year mourning period is over, the fire may be extinguished. Zizi said, "If you were to eat fine rice and wear patterned silk, would you feel at ease?
If you feel at ease, then do it. However, when a gentleman dwells in mourning, he finds fine food tasteless, hears music without joy, and his dwelling is uneasy;
therefore, he does not do these things. Now that you feel at ease, you may do them. After Zai Wo had left, Zizi said, "I underestimated him."
"Benevolence! A child is born, and only after three years is it finally released from the parents' embrace.
The three-year mourning period is the universal mourning practice of the world; do I, too, not have three years of love for my parents?
Although this section discusses Zai Yu’s inquiry and concludes with a stern rebuke by Confucius, the commentator [Xiang Kai] has cited this passage from the *Analects* as the primary authority.
The Sūtra takes the fulfillment of filial piety as its fundamental principle.
Second, the comparison of the Sage’s virtue and the concluding eulogies both originate from the *Xiaojing shu* (Commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety);

the author borrows these as his own words to conclude the preceding text and offer a general praise. The first sentence refers to the "Chapter on the Three Powers," where Zengzi heard the five forms of filial piety.

Following these words of praise, the text immediately proceeds to the "Chapter on Sagely Governance," where it records that Zengzi asked, "May I venture to ask whether there is anything that surpasses filial piety in the virtue of a sage?
Here, the concluding response from that passage is used in its entirety; thus, it is clear that the sagely virtue does not exceed [filial piety].

Second, the explanation of the teaching. Part one: Distinguishing the differences between the [two] bodies in their preaching. Within this: first, citing the chapter; second, explaining the characteristics. Third:

first, generally citing the two bodies—since the Buddha-way is equal for all Buddhas, they all possess both true and manifested bodies, whether three or four, according to the appropriate opening or closing.
Next, from "Śākyamuni" onwards, specifically indicating the two teachings. That which was spoken by Śākyamuni is called "according to the capacity," beginning from the Deer Park...

From the finality of the Jetavana Garden to the beginning at the Śāla Grove, the Five Vehicles were first inaugurated and the Three Points were ultimately perfected. Whether vertical or horizontal, these teachings were detailed and subtle, intended to accord with the human mind;

yet because they could not allow for direct realization of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), that which was taught by Vairocana is designated as "ultimate," as indicated below in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Furthermore, works such as the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda* may also be subsumed under this category, rather than being restricted to the periods of the three or five [turnings of the wheel].

Regarding the "that which is subsumed," this refers to teaching directly according to the phenomena and principles of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) without conforming to the inclinations of sentient beings; thus, both the ancient records and the new commentaries offer this interpretation.

Master Zhiguan (Zhiyuan) arbitrarily claimed that the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) was merely taught by a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and therefore still belongs to the category of teaching according to [disciples'] capacities.

This is clearly because he was not well-versed in the intent of the sūtra. In his commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, Master Guifeng (Huiyuan), citing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the speaker of the teaching, states: "The Buddha... [is able to... [text fragment].
The epithet *Bhagavat* (Pójiābā), meaning "the destroyer of afflictions," refers precisely to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) by which the Dharmakāya is manifested.

Since the Pure Land is taught through the exposition of the Dharma, the *Dharmakāya*, and the *Saṃbhogakāya* are not distinct, this is not the *Nirmāṇakāya*. Is this not the True Body (*svābhāvikakāya*) teaching the *圆觉* (*Samantabhadra-jñāna*)?

*Śākyamuni* is fully called *Rocana*, also known as *Vairocana*; these are merely differences in the expansion or abbreviation of the Sanskrit sounds, as well as variations in their phonetic rendering, according to the Jin translation.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, the name Vairocana means "Light Shining Universally," for the two lights of body and wisdom pervade the entire dharma-realm;
it is also called "Fulfillment and Purity," because the coarse and subtle aspects of the two obstacles have been exhausted without exception.

The first [explanation] refers to the manifestation of qualities, while the second refers to the removal of obstacles. Although these two meanings differ, their essence is one and the same. However, regarding this...

The distinction between the provisional and the ultimate teachings is made by way of a general classification based on their meaning, as these two modes naturally exist within the adaptation to capacities.

For example, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three carts at the gate are provisional, while the ox-cart in the open space is ultimate. Thus, one knows that there are many ways to distinguish the provisional and the ultimate;
the present case also largely accords with what Master Yin established during the early Tang dynasty regarding the "winding path" and the "level road."

Regarding the two [categories] established by [the masters of the] Sui dynasty such as Yan and others—the gradual and the sudden; the "gradual" refers to that which was taught by Śākyamuni, while the "sudden" refers to that proclaimed by Vairocana.

The subsequent teaching is a general explanation of the meaning of the teachings (*śāsana*). Herein, the *sūtras* and *vinaya* are the "teachings that express" (*vyañjana-śāsana*), spoken by the two bodies of the True Transformation;
the "meanings expressed" (*artha*) are the wisdom, principle, virtues, and conduct, through which wisdom and principle cause one to awaken.

To explain their virtuous conduct, one should cause them to uphold the provisional teachings of the sutras and vinaya; while these differ from the ultimate meaning they convey, they are merely distinct in expression.
Second, citing the beginning and end to establish the proof: although the various teachings clarify filial piety extensively, I shall here cite only the beginning and the end.

In the interim, these must necessarily be complete; furthermore, when the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Brahmajāla*, and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras are compared and mutually illustrated, there are five points of significance:
first, since Śākyamuni, the transformation Buddha, preached what Śākyamuni, the true Buddha, had already taught;

Third, even if one provides the nourishment of the three sacrificial animals daily, yet fails to eliminate [vices], it is still unfilial. Now, those who consider themselves filial provide the three sacrificial animals daily;

The second point concerns what must be avoided: providing for them while performing evil deeds and failing to offer remonstrance is itself a form of compliance.

"Jīng" is explained as "dharma" and "constancy," meaning the tracks for the Way of a hundred kings and the virtuous models of a thousand generations.

Following these talismans, the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* discusses five meanings: first, "giving birth," because it gives birth to all meanings; second, "fountainhead," because its flavor and meaning overflow like a spring.
Third, it is called "manifestation" because it manifests all meanings; fourth, it is called "the carpenter's line" because it distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox;

Second, distinguishing the alternative names, general and specific, and their sequence, as explained in the preceding section, will be easy to understand.
Second, the correct explanation of the two parts: first, the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s introductory section of authentication (*śraddhā-varga*), which has two sub-sections:

The first question concerns on what basis the path of cultivation is established; the second question concerns who is to be taken as the teacher; the third question concerns by what means the ill-spoken Caraka was expelled and disciplined;

and the fourth question concerns what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras. The commentary cites the answers to these questions, while the notes regarding the contemplation of the body and so forth are to be understood as explained elsewhere.
Second, distinguishing and demonstrating [the meaning] in contrast with various sutras, which has two parts: first, a general citation of other sutras;
second, clarifying the differences regarding what is currently missing. Regarding the first, there are two parts:

first, clarifying what is missing; second, distinguishing the differences. Second, in distinguishing between existence and non-existence, the first part demonstrates that the present [state] lacks [a self], as all underlying intentions testify to the absence of self because views and pride have been exhausted.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ordinary beings possess three types of self: the self of views, the self of pride, and the self of names. Those in training possess two types;

although the self of views is absent, their afflictions of thought are not yet exhausted, so they still possess the self of pride. Those beyond training possess one type, as both views and pride have been exhausted."

It is merely a name; this follows from what appears later in other sutras. As for the "provisional existence" of the five aggregates, it refers to names established provisionally according to worldly convention, intended to distinguish them from views and conceit; thus it says, "not like the calculations of ordinary sentiment," and so forth.

Second, the detailed explanation of the two [types of hearing]. First, the explanation of the present text has five parts. First, regarding the three theories concerning what hears the doctrines of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:

first, it is said that the sense organ (*indriya*) hears; second, it is said that consciousness (*vijñāna*) hears; third, it is said that hearing is produced by the conjunction of the three—organ, object, and consciousness.

The third [theory] is exhaustive of the principle, and thus the Commentary (*Sūtra-śāstra*) employs it. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the ear-faculty is unimpaired and the sound is within the range of audibility..."
If one’s mind desires to hear, one hears immediately.

Regarding the two types of faith: first, the title is presented; second, from "Now, as for faith" (*fù xìn*) onwards, the characteristics are explained; finally, from "Thus, Zhaò... onwards, scriptural evidence is cited.
This is precisely how the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* provides its commentary.
Regarding the three periods [of time], the first two concern the correct interpretation. Within this, the first part provides a general explanation:

in all sutras, the phrase "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) is used because it refers to taking the beginning and the ultimate conclusion of the discourse as a single unit. As for "Master" (*śāstṛ*), it refers to the Dharma;

since the Buddha serves as a model for humans and devas, the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), in its section on the "Teacher Official" (*shizhi*), quotes Zheng Xuan as saying it is a term for one who teaches others through the Way. "Taking" (*zi*) means to receive; disciples take the Dharma as their standard.
Regarding the teacher, it is said that "the filial son [is such] because the good person is the teacher of the not-good person, and the not-good person is the resource for the good person.
The present statement refers to this: because the teacher’s exposition and the listener’s comprehension of the meaning of the teaching are complete and perfect, it is stated thus.

As for the exclusion of other times, this means it is not when other sūtras are being taught or when other matters are being performed. Next, as will be shown below, there are two reasons why the specific time periods are not clarified.
First, regarding the fact that the explanations of the sūtras are not uniform: there is no distinct substance [to time] apart from the states (*avasthā*) of matter and mind;

it is by way of these that time is elucidated. Thus, although there are infinite [distinctions], they are spoken of as "one" [time]. For example, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "At one time I was in the kingdom of Kāśī;
at one time I was on the bank of the Ganges; at one time I was in the Śīrṣavana forest," and so forth. Second, it is categorized according to regions.

Regarding the "indefinite" (aniyata) explanation: the terminology for the various directions includes both vertical and horizontal; "vertical" refers to above and below, while "horizontal" refers to the four cardinal directions.

As for "prolongation and contraction," fifty human years constitute one day and night in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), and so forth. There are two interpretations of this "indefinite":

first, it is called indefinite because it specifically refers to the aforementioned prolongation and contraction; second, it means that the days and nights differ across the four continents (*caturdvīpa*).

Therefore, it is said that [the seasons] are indeterminate; for instance, when it is midnight in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), it is midday in the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa), sunset in the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha), and sunrise in the Western Continent (Aparagodānīya).

When the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, they were intended for circulation across all directions and the higher realms (*urdhva-dhātu*). If one were to speak of the four seasons based on a single location, they would not apply universally to all directions;
thus, he did not specify them individually. This is similar to how in India, the sixteenth day of the first month was taken as the beginning of the year.

Thus, while this [system] extends [the summer months] to the latter part of the year by taking the first day of the first month as the beginning of the year, that [system] shortens them to the earlier part;

furthermore, while this divides the year into four seasons, that divides it into six, and thus shortens [the seasonal periods]: (the period from the sixteenth of the first month until the onset of gradual heat;

from the sixteenth of the third month until the height of the heat; from the sixteenth of the fifth month until the rainy season; from the sixteenth of the seventh month until the time of lush growth; from the sixteenth of the ninth month until the onset of cold; and from the sixteenth of the eleventh month until the height of the cold). Moreover, that...

In secular tradition, time is sometimes divided into four seasons, whereas in Buddhism it is divided into three: the period for removing heat begins on the sixteenth day of the first month, the period for removing summer heat begins on the sixteenth day of the fifth month, and the period for removing cold begins on the sixteenth day of the ninth month.

Furthermore, they divide the day and night into eight periods (four for the day and four for the night), with each period further subdivided into four parts, as described in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions).
Since these divisions vary according to the specific region and are not fixed, we shall here speak only of the twelve divisions beginning with Zi and Chou.
It is for only a single moment.
Second, the removal of objections has two parts: first, restating the objection;

second, the response and explanation. Regarding the first, the commentary cites the interpretations of others: as for the phrase "some say" (*yathāha*) and so forth, since the preceding section provided the correct explanation, it simply stated "one."
At that time, the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) further first employed the words of others to reveal why the sūtra’s author did not necessarily specify the time, thereby resolving that objection:

In this way, whether the retribution and transformation [bodies] are distant or near, sharp or dull, long or short, their excellence is contained within. Master Zhizhen of Zhiyuan Garden recklessly claimed that this was indicated in the commentary.

[The critic] plucks at the flowers while losing the meaning of the text, yet forcibly constructs these successive layers of difficult arguments. However, there is an explanation for this:

the reference to "benevolent grace" and "refined elegance" actually derives from the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Rebirth Above* (*Shangsheng jing shu*). Alas, the religious teachings of that school were widely prevalent in the capital. What a pity!
I, Zhiguan, have not yet seen this.
The second [section] correctly indicates that the current explanation of the names of the sixteen kingdoms is derived from the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
1. Aṅga; 2. Magadha; 3. Kāśi; 4. Kośala; 5. Vṛji; 6. Malla; 7. Ceti; 8. Vatsa; 9. Ni... [The text continues with the remaining names.]
